A long bronze frieze above Tahrir Square, Liberation Square, in the centre of Baghdad, unveiled in 1961. It celebrates the 14 July Revolution of 1958, which overthrew the monarchy and made Iraq a republic.

The new leader Abd al-Karim Qasim commissioned it from the sculptor Jawad Saleem, who worked on it with his wife, the British-born artist Lorna Selim. Saleem died early in 1961, before it was finished.

The bronze figures stand on a travertine wall high above the square. Read from right to left, like Arabic writing, they tell a story: oppression and protest, then a soldier breaking the bars of a prison at the centre, then peace, farming and plenty. The flat, carved figures consciously echo the stone reliefs of Assyria and Babylon, joined to modern art.

It became the best known landmark of modern Iraqi art. In the protests of 2019 crowds gathered under it, and it became their symbol.
sum: A long bronze frieze above Tahrir Square, Liberation Square, in the centre of Baghdad, unveiled in 1961. It celebrates the 14 July Revolution of 1958, which overthrew the monarchy and made Iraq a republic.
